papers.title: Resolving the Mobility-Equity-Emissions Trilemma: A Causal Machine Learning Framework for Dynamic Tolling Policy
papers.abstract: We propose a causal machine learning framework to integrate dynamic tolling for mobility, equity, and climate objectives, resolving a long-standing policy trilemma. Using Double Machine Learning, we estimate zone-type-specific treatment effects, showing that commercial zones yield nearly twice the delay reduction of residential zones. Our adaptive quota mechanism expands residential coverage 34-fold while preserving 93% of total delay savings and sustaining high return on investment. The framework delivers climate co-benefits, reducing emissions by 743.5 metric tons of CO2 (valued at 141 USD) via congestion-sensitive pricing under moderate traffic conditions with sensitivity bounds from 557.6 to 929.3 tons. Crucially, we uncover a policy-invariant toll range where performance remains robust across demand scenarios, simplifying implementation. This study reveals critical, previously unidentified insights, such as a policy-invariant toll range, that can significantly simplify real-world implementation. Validated on synthetic data mirroring real-world networks, our methodological advances lay the foundation for future public deployment.

papers.title: Heterogeneity and Subgrouping in Modern Statistics and AI
papers.abstract: Heterogeneity is a defining feature of modern data: individuals, subpopulations, sites, modalities, tasks, and time points may differ in distributions, associations, treatment effects, or decision objectives. This review develops a unified perspective in which heterogeneous analysis is a problem of structured information borrowing: deciding what should be shared, what should remain distinct, and how uncertainty about that structure should enter inference and decisions. We connect classical stratification, interaction models, finite mixtures, mixed-effects models, and empirical Bayes with subgroup discovery, individualized learning, synthetic data generation, large language models, federated learning, privacy, security, and mobile health. Precision medicine provides a central example: subgroup rules offer interpretable approximations to individualized response surfaces, whereas partially pooled models stabilize patient-specific estimation. Across applications, the same tensions recur: population averages can conceal consequential variation, unrestricted personalization is unstable, adaptive subgroup discovery creates selection bias, and borrowing across incompatible sources causes negative transfer. These difficulties are amplified in contemporary AI, where sparse user histories, entangled representations, heterogeneous preferences, feedback loops, distribution shift, and privacy constraints make reliable personalization and evaluation especially challenging. We conclude with an agenda for calibrated personalization that integrates multilevel representations, selective borrowing, subgroup-aware evaluation, and valid uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: Movement synchronization in complex and dynamic team coordination
papers.abstract: Mutual anticipation of teammates' actions enables efficient coordination that achieves a common goal and high performance. In team sports involving direct competition, such implicit and nonverbal interactions within short periods are required. If players begin moving after observing their teammates, gaps may emerge, allowing opponents to interfere. When mutual anticipation functions appropriately, players' interactions are smooth without gaps, and their movements are expected to become synchronized. Synchronization represents a temporally stable structure whose mechanisms have been examined. However, few studies have investigated synchronization in complex and dynamic real-world coordination involving heterogeneous roles and evolving interactions within short periods. The examinations have been essentially limited to determining whether there are statistical differences from a baseline. In our approach, we utilized team sports and introduced a statistical method to provide detailed probabilistic evaluations of these differences. The purpose of this study was to extract the temporal components of movement using 3-on-3 basketball. In a field experiment investigating offensive coordination, we calculated the relative phases in which players approached or moved away from their teammates during mini-games. The frequency distributions were estimated using Bayesian inference and compared before and after receiving advice from the coach. The results showed that the posterior probabilities that the frequencies in synchronization-related bins were higher after the advice than before the advice were 70\% or higher. As a pilot study, these findings may provide a first step toward understanding coordination processes related to mutual anticipation based on a common ground of team strategy.
